title: Graphs, traversal, and shortest-path reasoning
masterChecklist: Searching, sorting, hashing, heaps, trees, graphs, shortest paths, traversals, union-find, tries
Core data structures: arrays/lists, stacks, queues, dequeues, hash tables, linked structures, priority queues, trees, graphs
Correctness reasoning, edge cases, algorithm engineering and trade-off communication
whyItMatters: Many real problems are relationships rather than rows: pages linking to pages, lessons depending on lessons, services calling services, or stations connected by routes. Graph thinking makes those relationships explicit.
simpleExplanation: A graph has nodes and edges. Breadth-first search (BFS) explores all nearby nodes before going farther away. In an unweighted graph, that means the first time BFS reaches a node it has found a route with the fewest edges. A visited set prevents loops from being explored forever.
mentalModel: Imagine passing a message through friends. BFS tells every direct friend first, then friends-of-friends. A visited list stops the message from bouncing around the same circle forever.
outcomes: Represent a small graph with a dictionary of neighbor lists.
Use a queue and visited set for BFS.
Explain when unweighted shortest path means fewest edges.
Name edge cases such as a missing start node or disconnected graph.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learner dashboard recommends the next reachable lesson from a prerequisite map.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A cyclic prerequisite mistake can make a naive traversal loop forever, and a missing prerequisite can cause a KeyError.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Validate nodes, track visited nodes, define a policy for disconnected content, and use BFS only when each edge has equal cost.

explanation: deque makes removing the next queued item clear and efficient for this use.
visited is updated when a node is queued, preventing duplicate queue entries.
The loop processes nearby lessons before more distant lessons.
The missing-start policy returns an empty list in this example; a different application may raise a clear error.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add 'start' as a neighbor of functions. The output still terminates because start is already visited.

procedure: Define what nodes and edges mean in the domain.
Choose adjacency lists for a small sparse graph.
Define behavior for missing, duplicate, and disconnected nodes.
Use a queue for BFS and mark nodes visited when discovered.
Use a weighted algorithm only when edge costs differ and test against small hand-drawn graphs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Marking a node visited only after removing it from the queue.
commonMistakes.why: Several parents can queue the same node before it is processed.
commonMistakes.avoid: Mark it visited at discovery time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using BFS as a cost-optimal algorithm when edges have different weights.
commonMistakes.why: Fewest edges is not necessarily the cheapest total cost.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use an appropriate weighted shortest-path algorithm and data structure.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every referenced neighbor exists as a graph key.
commonMistakes.avoid: Validate graph shape or use a documented missing-node policy.

lab.title: Traverse a fictional lesson prerequisite graph
lab.safety: Uses only small local dictionaries of fictional lesson names.
guidedSteps: While the queue has items, remove the leftmost node.
For each unvisited neighbor, mark it and append it.
lab.solutionExplanation: The queue creates breadth-first order, while the visited set prevents repeated work and cycles.
challenges: Predict the order for the starter graph.
Experiment: add a cycle and confirm the result terminates.
lab.testCode:
graph = {'start': ['lists', 'loops'], 'lists': ['functions'], 'loops': ['functions'], 'functions': []}
assert reachable('start', graph) == ['start', 'lists', 'loops', 'functions']
assert reachable('missing', graph) == []
assert reachable('functions', graph) == ['functions']
print('PASS: breadth-first visitation')

projectConnection.milestone: Represent lesson prerequisites, find reachable lessons safely, and document the policy for cycles and missing nodes.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: Your traversal terminates on a cycle and you can explain why BFS is appropriate only for equal-cost edges.

assessment.question: What two parts define a graph?
assessment.explanation: The meaning of each comes from the domain model.

assessment.question: Why use a visited set in BFS?
assessment.answer: To avoid revisiting nodes and to terminate on cycles.

assessment.question: When does BFS find a shortest path in edge count?
assessment.answer: When every edge is treated as equal cost in an unweighted graph.
assessment.explanation: Different costs require a different algorithm.
